summary: Specifies a protocol for encapsulating an arbitrary network layer protocol inside another arbitrary network layer protocol. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) carries one network-layer packet inside another protocol's packet. Its header identifies the inner packet type and can include a checksum, while an outer delivery protocol carries it to the tunnel endpoint.

subtitle: A general header for carrying one network-layer packet inside another.

tldr.problem: Separate encapsulation protocols were needed for many pairings of network protocols, making the number of special cases difficult to manage.
tldr.mechanism: GRE places a header between an outer delivery protocol and a payload packet. The header identifies the payload protocol and can include an optional checksum.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2784 specifies the deployed GRE version 0 format. It has been updated by RFC 2890 and RFC 9601; the document leaves IPv6 delivery and payload, Path MTU Discovery, and other interactions open.

today: RFC 2784 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2000. It has been updated by RFC 2890 and RFC 9601.

sections.title: A General Packet Encapsulation
sections.content:
GRE is a general protocol for encapsulating one network-layer protocol inside another. The packet being carried is the payload packet; it is placed inside a GRE packet, which can then be carried by an outer delivery protocol. The RFC describes the common GRE behavior deployed by multiple vendors.

The design aims to reduce the need for a separate encapsulation specification for every protocol pairing. It does not define when a packet should be encapsulated, and it may be less suitable where a protocol-specific encapsulation already exists.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE adds a common wrapper around a packet so another network protocol can carry it. The choice of which packets to wrap is left to other mechanisms.

sections.title: Layers in a GRE Packet
sections.content:
A GRE-encapsulated packet has an outer delivery header, a GRE header, and the payload packet. The GRE header identifies the payload protocol. The delivery protocol is responsible for carrying the resulting packet to the other endpoint.

The base GRE header contains a checksum-present bit, reserved bits, a version field, and a 2-octet Protocol Type. A checksum and a reserved field follow only when the checksum-present bit is set.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer protocol carries the packet, GRE identifies what is inside, and the payload is the original packet. The checksum fields are present only when the header's checksum bit is set.

sections.title: Version, Protocol Type, and Checksum
sections.content:
The GRE version field must be zero. The Protocol Type identifies the payload using ETHER TYPE values; a receiver should discard a packet with a type not listed in the referenced ETHER TYPE registries. Reserved bits 6 through 12 must be sent as zero and ignored when received. A receiver that does not implement RFC 1701 must discard packets with any of bits 1 through 5 set.

If the checksum-present bit is one, the packet includes a 2-octet checksum and a 2-octet Reserved1 field. The checksum is the IP one's-complement checksum over the GRE header and payload, computed with the checksum field set to zero. Reserved1 must be sent as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The header names the inner protocol and its GRE version. When present, the checksum covers both the GRE header and payload, while reserved fields must remain zero.

sections.title: Carrying and Forwarding IPv4
sections.content:
When IPv4 is the payload, the GRE Protocol Type must be 0x800. After decapsulation, the tunnel endpoint forwards the inner IPv4 packet using its destination address and decrements its TTL. If that destination is the encapsulator at the other end of the tunnel, the endpoint must discard the packet to prevent a loop.

When GRE itself is carried over IPv4, IPv4 protocol number 47 identifies it as the delivery payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel endpoint removes the GRE wrapper and forwards the inner IPv4 packet toward its destination. It decreases the packet's TTL and discards a packet addressed back to the tunnel endpoint.

sections.title: Interoperation with RFC 1701
sections.content:
RFC 1701 used bits now called Reserved0 as flags for optional key, sequence-number, routing, and strict-source-route fields. RFC 2784 deprecates those fields and specifies that its GRE headers do not contain them.

A sender following RFC 2784 sets Reserved0 to zero, which an RFC 1701 receiver interprets as no optional fields. Conversely, a receiver that does not implement RFC 1701 discards packets with any of bits 1 through 5 set, rather than misreading an older extended header.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 2784 leaves the older optional fields unused. A receiver that does not support the older format rejects packets that mark those fields as present.

sections.title: Filtering and Known Limitations
sections.content:
Routing with GRE follows IPv4 routing, but packet filtering may need to inspect the encapsulated packet or run at the tunnel endpoints. The RFC notes that a tunnel may be terminated at a firewall when filtering inside GRE is a concern.

The appendix lists issues outside this specification, including Path MTU Discovery, IPv6 as a delivery or payload protocol, interaction with ICMP and differentiated services, and multiple or looping encapsulations. Existing IPv4-delivered GRE implementations described by the RFC do not implement Path MTU Discovery or set the Don't Fragment bit.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall may need to inspect the inner packet or filter traffic at a tunnel endpoint. The RFC also lists packet-size behavior, IPv6 support, and other interactions as unresolved topics.
